title: Chapter 6: Making Decisions: if, elif and else
video_title: Python Chapter 6: Making Decisions, if, elif and else
summary: Asha's bill splitter crashed with zero people and treated every customer the same. Follow her as she makes her cafe checkout decide: comparisons, if, else, elif and boundary values, and, or and not, and safe text answers. Then watch her build a free-biscuit rule with an AI assistant at all six stages, catching two AI mistakes with edge-case tests.

visual.heading: Today's mission: a checkout that decides

A login page lets you in only when the password matches. Each one checks a fact, and then chooses what to do.

scenes.title: The idea: conditions are True or False
scenes.direction: Teach comparison operators with the table, then the if diagram, then the gate analogy. Then a quiz on the boundary, then a breather.

visual.heading: Six comparison operators
visual.label: The idea
rows: is less than or equal to
is greater than or equal to

segments.say: A condition is a question that Python answers with True or False. You met True and False in Chapter 2. They are the two values of the type bool.
Double equals asks: are these two values equal? Exclamation mark equals asks the opposite: are they different?
Less than, and greater than. Look closely: 15 is not greater than 15, so that one is False.
Add an equals sign, and the value itself is included. 15 is greater than or equal to 15, so this one is True.
And remember: one equals sign gives a name a value. Two equals signs ask a question.

visual.heading: if runs a block only when it is True
visual.label: The idea
body: The **block** is the group of indented lines under the line that ends with a colon.
visual.pre:
if people == 0:                      <- condition, then a colon
      print("Please type 1 or more.")  <- the block: 4 spaces in
  print("Thank you!")                  <- not indented: always runs

          people == 0 ?
           /        \
        True        False
          |           |
   run the block   skip it
           \        /
     continue with the next line

segments.say: An if statement asks a condition. If the answer is True, Python runs the block. If it is False, Python skips it.
The block is the group of lines that are indented, four spaces in, under the line that ends with a colon.
The last line is not indented, so it always runs.

visual.heading: A condition is like a gate
visual.label: Analogy
items: A gate at the cafe door checks one fact: is this person a member?
True: the gate opens. False: it stays closed.
Unlike a person, the gate cannot guess: `"Yes"` and `"yes"` are different answers.

segments.say: Think of a gate at the cafe door. It checks one fact: is this person a member? True, it opens. False, it stays closed.
But unlike a person at a door, the gate cannot guess. Yes with a capital Y and yes with a small y are two different answers.

visual.question: `to_pay` is exactly `15`. Which condition is `True`?
visual.explain: `>=` includes the value itself, so 15 >= 15 is True.

segments.say: Quick check. To pay is exactly 15. Which of these conditions is True?

after.say: C. Greater than or equal to. The equals sign includes 15 itself.

items: A condition is `True` or `False`.
`==` asks; one `=` gives a value.
`if` runs its indented block only when `True`.

segments.say: Take a breather. Here is what you know so far.
Next, Asha asks Python her first questions.

scenes.title: Step 1: Compare values
scenes.direction: Each comparison is explained before the prediction. Reveal the output after the question.

segments.say: Step 1. Asha stores the tea price, 3.5. Line 3 asks: is it greater than 3?
Line 4 asks if it equals 3.5, and line 5 asks if it is different from 3.5.
Line 6 asks if it is less than or equal to 3. Line 7 compares two words.
And line 8 asks for the type of a comparison.

ask.question: What do line 5 and line 7 print?

after.say: Lines 3 and 4 are True. Line 5 is False, because the price is not different from 3.5.
Line 7 is False too. Tea with a capital T and tea with a small t are different text, like the gate.
And line 8 shows the type of a comparison: bool.

scenes.title: Step 2: if
scenes.direction: The file types in. Teach the colon and the block, then ask which lines run for the typed answer 0.

visual.heading: Step 2: Run a block only when it is True

segments.say: Step 2. Line 2 asks for the number of people. Line 3 is the if: the condition, people equals 0, and then a colon.
Lines 4 and 5 are indented. They are the block.
Line 6 is not indented. It is outside the block.

ask.question: The user types `0`. Which lines print?

after.say: The condition is True, so both lines of the block run, and then line 6.
Type 4 instead, and the condition is False. Python skips the block, and prints only: Thank you.

scenes.title: Step 3: else
scenes.direction: Call back to the Chapter 5 crash. Teach that exactly one of two blocks runs, ask, then reveal.

segments.say: Step 3. This is the fix for the bill splitter's crash. Line 4 asks: is the number of people greater than 0? If so, lines 5 and 6 share the bill.
Line 7 says else. Its block runs when the condition is False.
Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both. Then line 9 runs either way.

ask.question: The user types `0` people. Does line 5, the division, run?

after.say: No. 0 is not greater than 0, so the condition is False. Python jumps to the else block.
The division never happens, so there is no crash. A clear message instead, and then Done.

scenes.title: Step 4: elif and boundary values
scenes.direction: Teach elif as a ladder checked from the top, ask about the boundary value, then explain why order matters.

segments.say: Step 4. The cafe has two rewards. A free cake for 50 or more, on lines 3 and 4.
Elif means else if. Lines 5 and 6 give a free biscuit for 15 or more.
And the else block catches everything else.
Python checks from the top, and runs only the first block whose condition is True. Then it skips the rest.

ask.question: The customer pays exactly `15`. Which reward prints?

after.say: A free biscuit. Line 3 is False, because 15 is less than 50. Line 5 is True, because greater than or equal includes 15.
Exactly 15 is a boundary value: the point where the result changes. And notice the order: the biggest amount comes first. It matters later today.

scenes.title: Step 5: and, or, not
scenes.direction: Teach the three rules first, then predict two lines, reveal, then a quiz and a breather.

segments.say: Step 5. Sometimes one fact is not enough. And is True only when both sides are True.
Or is True when at least one side is True.
And not turns True into False, and False into True.

visual.heading: Step 5: and, or, not in action

segments.say: Asha is a member, but she pays only 12.
Line 5 joins two facts with and. Line 6 joins the same two facts with or.

ask.question: What do line 5 and line 6 print?

after.say: Line 5 is False. She is a member, but 12 is not 15 or more, and and needs both.
Line 6 is True. Or needs only one, and she is a member.
Line 7, not a member, is False. And line 8 is True, because the day is Friday. Each side of or needs a full comparison.

visual.question: `is_member` is `False` and `to_pay` is `20`. What is `is_member or to_pay >= 15`?
visual.explain: `or` needs only one side: 20 >= 15 is True.

segments.say: Quick check. Is member is False, and to pay is 20. What is: is member, or to pay greater than or equal to 15?

after.say: A. True. The customer is not a member, but 20 is 15 or more, and or needs only one side.

items: `else` runs when the condition is `False`.
Python runs the first `elif` that is `True`.
`and` needs both; `or` needs one.

segments.say: Breather. Roll your shoulders, and take a slow breath.
One more piece, and Asha's checkout is ready: answers typed by real people.

scenes.title: Step 6: Safe text answers
scenes.direction: Teach strip and lower on the answer, then ask about the typed answer with a capital and a space, then reveal.

visual.heading: Step 6: Compare text answers safely
visual.note: The user will type: Yes  (with a space at the end)

segments.say: Step 6. Real people type Yes, or yes, or yes with a space at the end. To the gate, those are all different.
So line 3 cleans the answer first. Strip removes the spaces at both ends. Lower makes every letter small, as in Chapter 3.
Only then does it compare with yes, in small letters.

ask.question: The user types `Yes ` with a capital Y and a space. Is the condition on line 3 `True`?

after.say: Yes, it is True. After strip and lower, the answer is exactly yes. So the member discount prints.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the checkout that decides
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Explain every group of lines, ask about the reward for Asha's answers, reveal. Hand over to the AI story.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the checkout
visual.note: The user will type: Asha, then 6, then Yes

segments.say: Back to the mission. Lines 2 to 4 ask the questions. Line 4 cleans the member answer straight away, with strip and lower.
Line 6 works out the bill: the number of teas times 3.5.
Lines 7 to 10 decide the discount. Members get 10 percent. Everyone else gets a discount of 0.
Line 11 takes the discount away, and lines 13 to 15 print the bill.
Lines 16 to 19 decide the reward: a biscuit for 15 or more.

ask.question: Asha types `6` teas and `Yes`. Does she get the free biscuit?

after.say: Six teas cost 21.00. She is a member, so the discount is 2.10.
She pays 18.90. That is 15 or more, so yes: a free biscuit!
Mission complete! Now Asha wants to be sure her biscuit rule is right. She uses an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one rule
scenes.direction: Teach the edge case skill first. Then one conversation per stage, all about the free-biscuit rule. Stage 3 plants the boundary mistake; stage 4 catches it; stage 6 catches a wrong order.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: edge cases
visual.label: Before you start
items: An **edge case** is an unusual input that can break a condition.
Boundary values, zero, and answers with capitals or spaces are edge cases.
Ask AI for the edge cases, then run every one. Never paste private data.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is asking for edge cases: unusual inputs that can break a condition, like exactly 15, zero, or a capital letter.
Ask the AI to list them, then run every one. And the safety habits from Chapter 1 still apply.

visual.heading: Plan: the rule and its boundary values

messages.text: I am a beginner learning if. My cafe gives a free biscuit when the amount to pay is 15 or more. Do not write code yet. List the condition in words, and the boundary values I should test, with the result for each.

1. The condition: the amount to pay is 15 or more.
2. Test 14.99: no biscuit.
3. Test 15: a biscuit. This is the boundary value, where the result changes.
4. Test 20: a biscuit.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha describes the biscuit rule in words, and asks for the boundary values to test. No code yet.
The AI lists 14.99, 15 and 20, with the result for each. 15 is the boundary value, where the result changes.

visual.heading: Write it yourself, then check the boundary

messages.text: I wrote the condition myself. Do not change it. Does the block run when to_pay is exactly 15? Which operator decides it?
Yes. `>=` means greater than or equal to, so the value 15 itself is included. The block runs and prints the reward.
I ran it with 15.0, and it agrees:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes the condition herself, with greater than or equal. She asks the AI what happens at exactly 15.
The AI explains that greater than or equal includes 15 itself.
Asha runs it with 15.0. The reward prints. The explanation and the real run agree.

visual.heading: Generate: ask for an exact prediction

messages.text: Now write the full rule with an else: 'Reward: a free biscuit' for 15 or more, otherwise 'No biscuit this time'. If to_pay is exactly 15.0, tell me exactly what it prints.
Here is the code. For 15.0 it prints `Reward: a free biscuit`.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Now Asha wants the full rule, with an else. She asks the AI for the code, and for exactly what it prints at 15.0.
The AI writes five lines, and says: a free biscuit. It sounds completely sure.
Look at line 3 carefully.

ask.question: The AI says this prints `Reward: a free biscuit` for 15.0. Is it right?

after.say: Asha runs it. No biscuit this time! The AI was wrong, and it sounded sure.

messages.text: You predicted a biscuit for 15.0, but it printed 'No biscuit this time'. Which edge case did your code fail, and why?
The boundary value, 15.0. Line 3 uses `>`, which means more than, so 15 is not included. Use `>=`:

segments.say: Stage 4: test. The boundary value, 15, was exactly the test from the plan. Asha tells the AI what it predicted, and what really happened.
Now the AI names the cause. Greater than means more than, so 15 is left out. The fix is greater than or equal.
Asha runs the fix with 15.0. A free biscuit. Prediction and real run agree.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I typed the rule into my checkout and got this error. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

Line 3 uses one `=`, which gives a name a value. A condition must compare. Your rule is 15 or more, so write:
`if to_pay >= 15:`

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha types the rule into her checkout, but with one equals sign. Python stops with a Syntax Error, before any line runs.
She asks for the cause first. The AI points to line 3. One equals sign gives a value. A condition must compare.

messages.text: Here are my reward rules. Suggest at most two improvements for readability, each with one reason. Do not change what it prints for any amount.

1. Add a comment above the rules: `# Rewards: cake for 50 or more, biscuit for 15 or more`.
2. Check the biscuit rule first, because it is the most common reward.
Before I change anything, I will test suggestion 2 with a big amount, 60.0.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. The rewards work. Asha asks for at most two readability improvements that do not change the output.
Suggestion 1, a comment, helps a reader. Suggestion 2 says: check the biscuit rule first, because it is the most common.
Remember the order from step 4? Asha does not trust it yet. She tests it with a big amount, 60.

visual.heading: Testing suggestion 2 with 60.0
visual.hidden_text: Predict the reward for 60.0 before it appears.

segments.say: Here is the suggested order. The biscuit rule on line 3 comes first. The cake rule on line 5 comes second.

ask.question: To pay is `60.0`. Which reward prints?

after.say: A free biscuit, not a cake! 60 is 15 or more, so line 3 is True first, and Python never checks line 5.
The AI was wrong again. Asha keeps her order, with the biggest amount first, and adds only the comment.

visual.question: The rule is "15 or more". Which test value catches `>` written instead of `>=`?
visual.explain: 15 is the boundary value: `>` and `>=` give different results only there.

segments.say: Quick check. The rule is 15 or more. Which test value catches greater than written instead of greater than or equal?

after.say: B. 15, the boundary value. That is the only value where the two operators disagree.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
Test the boundary value every time.
In an elif ladder, the biggest amount comes first.

segments.say: Breather. Asha caught two AI mistakes, with two things you learned today: boundary values, and the elif order.
Next, the four mistakes beginners make most with if. You have already met the first one.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 calls back to the debug stage. Mistakes 3 and 4 are spot-it questions on rules taught earlier. Then a summary table and a quiz.

segments.say: Mistake 1 is the one Asha debugged. One equals sign in a condition.
The message even suggests the fix: double equals. You can ignore the other suggestion. This course does not use it.
Mistake 2. Every if, elif and else line ends with a colon. Here, line 3 has none.
The message says exactly that: expected a colon. The small arrow points to where it should be.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Remember how Python knows which lines belong to the block.

after.say: Line 4 is not indented, so the if on line 3 has no block. Python reports an Indentation Error.
after.heading: Mistake 3: a block that is not indented

after.say: The fix: indent line 4 by four spaces. Most code editors do it for you after the colon.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the reason before the answer appears.

segments.say: One more. Asha is a member, and the answer stored on line 2 is Yes. Think of the gate.

ask.question: Asha is a member. Why does this program print `No discount`?

after.say: Yes with a capital Y is not equal to yes with a small y. No error at all, a wrong result, and a member pays too much.
after.heading: Mistake 4: capital letters in a text answer

after.say: The fix is the one from step 6: compare the answer after strip and lower.

items: `==` compares; `:` ends the line.
Indent the block by 4 spaces.
Clean text answers before you compare them.

segments.say: Last breather. These errors will not surprise you any more.
Two questions to think about on your own come next.

visual.question: The biscuit is only for members who pay 15 or more. Which word joins the two conditions?
visual.hint: test it with a member who pays 12, and a visitor who pays 20.

segments.say: First. Asha wants the free biscuit only for members who pay 15 or more. Which word joins the two conditions?

after.say: Write it, then test it with a member who pays 12, and a visitor who pays 20.

visual.question: Some customers type `y` instead of `yes`. How could one condition accept both?

segments.say: Second. Some customers type y, instead of yes. How could one condition accept both answers?

after.say: Predict which answers still fail, then test them.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then a final quick check, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A condition works out to `True` or `False`, the two values of `bool`.
`==` compares. One `=` gives a name a value.
`if` runs its indented block only when the condition is `True`; `else` when it is `False`.
Python runs only the first `elif` block that is `True`, so order matters.
`and`, `or` and `not` combine conditions. Compare text after `.strip().lower()`.
Ask AI for edge cases, such as boundary values, and run every one.

segments.say: Let's recap.
A condition works out to True or False, the two values of bool.
Double equals compares. One equals sign gives a name a value.
If runs its indented block only when the condition is True, and else runs when it is False.
Only the first True elif block runs, so order matters. And, or, and not combine conditions. Clean text answers before you compare them.
And with AI: ask for the edge cases, and run every one.

visual.question: `to_pay` is `60`. The first rule checks `>= 15` (biscuit), then `elif >= 50` (cake). What prints?
visual.explain: Python runs only the first True block: 60 >= 15 comes first.

segments.say: One last check. To pay is 60. The first rule checks 15 or more, for a biscuit. The elif checks 50 or more, for a cake. What prints?

after.say: C. A free biscuit. Only the first True block runs. That is why the biggest amount goes first.
